Formalizing Popular Science Using Middle Way Mathematics to Describe Quantum Statistical Mechanics

Modern physical theories—such as quantum mechanics, relativity, and thermal physics—present a challenge for popular science: these theories are described by mathematical concepts requiring limit theory, measure theory, differential geometry, and functional analysis, among other disciplines, which take years or study to master. So popular science routinely asks readers to appreciate these theories through qualitative prose, metaphorical analogies, and informal illustrations. 

The alternative is to streamline the mathematics. This site uses Middle Way Mathematics (MWM) to formalize quantum statistical mechanics for the general reader. It provides a mathematical runway—from single-sorted classical logic, ZF set theory, recursive number trees, and infinitesimals to state spaces, entropy, and quantum density operators—and it will describe quantum statistical mechanics formally, using MWM.

Quantum statistical mechanics is chosen because of it's relationship to everyday phenomenological experience. Particle physics may be fundamental, but the behavior observed is on a scale that is difficult to relate to; and although general relativity is an elegant use of differential geometry, the only phenomenon described is gravity. In any case, a formal understanding of quantum statistical mechanics is a worthy if ambitious goal.

Of course, as popular science, the understanding will be brittle, and will lack the depth to be of much practical use, as is the way of popular science.

Across the lecture series, the dialogues trace a deliberate developmental progression: in the early lectures, Jill explores logic and numbers as an inquisitive child in elementary school; by the final series on quantum statistical mechanics, she is engaging with modern physics at a university level.

This arc directly reflects the conceptual architecture of Middle Way Mathematics:

  • The Foundations Are Simple: Starting with binary truth, counting spines, and Conway number trees requires no advanced academic preparation—the root ideas are so transparent that a young learner can grasp them directly through intuition and interactive exploration.
  • The Conceptual Sophistication Escalates Naturally: As the lectures advance into rates of change, Bayesian probability spaces, and non-commutative quantum density operators, the material matures in lockstep with the inquirer.

1. Epistemological Assumptions

Middle Way Mathematics (MWM) assumes mathematics, like propositional logic, is a formal science: syntax and rules are defined, assumptions are made, and one considers the implications.  MWM is assumed to model a slice of a mathematical reality, which is assumed to model aspects of a physical reality. The following diagram illustrates the notion that MWM formalizes a mathematical model of a certain physical theory, namely, a formal description of quantum statistical mechanics.


We side with Einstein: the moon really is there. We recognize that our relationship to physical reality is phenomenological, and if disciplined enough, empirical and quantitative. We acknowledge any relationships we assume to hold between phenomenological observables is subject to change. The following table lists some basic assumptions. 

Physical Reality & PhenomenaMathematical Formalisms & Models
• Objective and Independent: The physical universe unfolds independently of human observers, symbolic languages, or formal systems.

• Lived Phenomena: Tangible observations—the turning of a shadow, thermal diffusion through a solid, or photon polarization—form the primary empirical anchor.

• Non-Monotonic Discovery: Empirical knowledge is open to revision. A single reproducible experimental observation can overturn or reshape an accepted scientific model.		• Human Inventions: Scientific models—from Euclidean geometry to quantum density operators (ρ)—are formal tools developed to organize and predict observations.

• Deductive Precision: Mathematical deduction is monotonic. Theorems formally derived from established axioms remain permanently valid within their specified domain.

• Monotonic description of Non-Monotonic logic: A formal description of Non-Monotonic Discovery.

Improvements to physical theories often mirror improvements to the underlying mathematical representations. For example, over four millennia the concept of angle has been formulated as a builder's slope, a geometric chord, a half-chord (sine), an arc length (radian), and an algebraic rotor. None of these is the physical phenomenon of turning itself; each is a mathematical tool suited to specific analytical tasks. In MWM, representing numbers and angles via directed paths on recursive trees is chosen because it enables exact, discrete calculation while remaining conceptually transparent.

2. The Evolution of Physical State Spaces

Over the past four centuries, mathematical physics advanced by shifting where physical reality is modeled to reside—progressing from direct spatial geometry to abstract, high-dimensional state spaces:

Historical Era Where Reality Is Modeled to Live State Representation
1. Direct Physical Space
(Newton, 17th c.)		 3D Euclidean Space: ℝ³ × ℝ Point particles with definite positions (x, y, z) evolving along continuous trajectories governed by vector forces.
2. Abstract State Spaces
(Lagrange & Hamilton, 18–19th c.)		 Configuration & Phase Spaces: Q × P The state of an entire physical system is a single point moving through an abstract energy phase space of positions and conjugate momenta.
3. Statistical Ensembles
(Boltzmann & Gibbs, 1870s)		 Probability Distributions over Microstates Macroscopic thermodynamic observables (temperature, pressure, entropy) emerge as statistical averages over microstate distributions.
4. Explanation Spaces
(Bayes, Boltzmann, Jaynes)		 Sample Space (Ω) & Belief Distributions Science is formalized as reasoning under uncertainty: candidate hypotheses assign probability distributions over states, updated via evidence.
5. Quantum State Space
(Planck, Born, von Neumann)		 Complex Hilbert Space (ℋ) & Density Operators (ρ) Physical states are complex probability amplitude vectors or statistical density operators satisfying unitary evolution and projection rules.

3. The Evolution of Mathematical Analysis 

 Mathematical analysis also evolved:

  • Intuitive Infinitesimals (17th–18th Century) — Leibniz, Newton, Euler:
    Calculus was invented using infinitesimals (dx, dy)—quantities strictly greater than zero yet smaller than any positive standard real number. Derivatives were algebraic ratios (dy / dx) and integrals were genuine sums of microscopic rectangles (∑ y · dx).
  • The Epsilon-Delta Approach (19th Century) — Cauchy, Weierstrass, Dedekind:
    Infinitesimals were banished due to a lack of formal foundations. They were replaced by static limit definitions involving epsilon and delta (ε–δ). While rigorous, this framework severed calculus from its intuitive operational roots and erected substantial pedagogical barriers.
  • The Topological Escape (Early–Mid 20th Century) — Hausdorff, Lebesgue, Bourbaki:
    Continuous mathematics shifted into point-set topology and abstract measure spaces. This provided powerful generality for functional analysis, but further distanced mathematics from constructive calculation.
  • Nonstandard Analysis — Abraham Robinson:
    Infinitesimals were given rigorous foundations via Robinson's nonstandard analysis.

4. streamlining mathematics

MWM does not depend on real numbers. This is the primary simplification to physical mathematics. 

The capstone of a firm foundation for an alternative to the real numbers was established in 2001 by van den Dries & Ehrlich:

  • (No(ε0), +, ·) is a totally ordered algebraic field where
    • No is the class generated by 2-successor transfinite induction
    • ε0 is the ordinal defined as the ω-high tower: ε0 := ωωω ·· where ω is the first nonfinite ordinal
    • total order is a recursively defined relation, and (+, ·) are recursively defined operations for addition and multiplication, as first described by John Conway circa 1970
    • and given that every member of the field (carrier) is associated with an ordinal-valued birthday, for a given ordinal α
      • No(α)  := {x ∈ No | x's birthday is less than α}

Note that ε0 is countable, and No(ε0) is a set, so (No(ε0), +, ·) is a field in a set theoretic sense. It is this constructed field that is recognized by MWM as mathematical fact. 

As ε0 is the smallest ordinal for which the constructed number set No(ε0) can serve as a carrier for a closed algebraic field, and it is impractical to perform an arithmetic calculation for arbitrary x, y ∈ No(ε0), MWM does not perform field level calculations. But fortunately

No(ω) ≅ (𝔻, +, ·)

where (𝔻, +, ·) is the Euclidean ring of dyadic rationals. This is our touchstone with numbers used in standard mathematics. MWM also considers the sets

ℝ_ω := No(ω+1)

𝔻_ω := 𝔻 ∪ {ω, 1/ω}

The set ℝ_ω ⊂ No(ε0) describes the members of  No(ε0) that may be used in MWM numeric expressions. ℝ_ω is not used as the carrier for algebraic structure. Although ℝ ⊂ ℝ_ω, (ℝ, +, ·) is not considered a subfield of (No(ε0), +, ·) because, to start,  (No(ε0), +, ·) has no subfields, and (No(ε0), +, ·) is not Archimedean. From the MWM perspective, the real Archimedean continuum of standard arithmetic, the bedrock of standard analysis, is a nonconstructive ideal. Anyway, the semantics of MWM numeric expressions is firmly rooted in the ambient background of the field (No(ε0), +, ·).  

On the other hand, the set 𝔻_ω is used as the carrier for an algebraic structure: the extended dyadic rationals, and the nonstandard ring of Laurent polynomials. This is the arena for all MWM calculation.

As ω, 1/ω =: dx ∈ ℝ_ω, the infinitesimal of nonstandard analysis, may appear in numeric expressions. But note that 1/ω and 1/3 share the exact same ontological status: they are both members of the set No(ε0) whose birthday is ω, and can be combined in an expression rooted in the field (No(ε0), +, ·) and the algebraic manipulation of these organic infinitesimals is the core of how MWM simplifies physical mathematics.

5 The Precision Evaluation Map

To calculate a numeric expression whose terms belong to ℝ_ω, MWM defines an explicit truncation function:

eval: exp(t:ℝ_ω) × ℕ → exp(t:{x ∈ 𝔻_ω | x < cutoff size(n ∈ ℕ)})

that prepares the expression for calculation. The evaluation map includes behavior similar to the standard part function of nonstandard analysis, but this occurs within the general framework of preparing a numeric expression for use in a calculation.

6 Summary of 2-successor case

In MWM (non-complex) number terms in numeric expressions are members of ℝ_ω. A precision evaluation map transforms such a expression to an expression whose number terms are dyadic rationals, as illustrated below.

7 The 4-Successor Tree: 2D Complex Plane & Infinitesimal Area

While 1D arithmetic is modeled along a 2-successor binary tree ({+1, -1}), 2D geometry is modeled on a 4-successor quadtree branching along orthogonal directions ({+1, -1, +i, -i}):

  • At finite stages (up to Day ω), the tree spans the Gaussian dyadics 𝔻[i] = { a + b·i | a, b ∈ 𝔻 }.
  • At stage ω+1, orthogonal branching establishes infinitesimal resolution in both axes: dx = 1/ω and dy = 1/ω.

The lectures construct this framework in five sequential series leading directly to Quantum Statistical Mechanics:

Series 1: Logic & Number

Single-sorted propositions, predicates, 2D relation matrices, and Conway number trees (ℕ, 𝔻, ℝ_ω).

Series 2: Algebraic Structure & Linearity

Sequences, arithmetic progressions, emergent groups, fields, vector spaces, and duality.

Series 3: Continuum & Calculus

Discrete analysis, 1D telescoping calculus, infinitesimal halos, and 2D complex plane analysis.

Series 4: Space, Angle & Transcendence

Rotor geometry on ℂ_ω, continuous exponential growth, natural logarithms, and scale reciprocity.

Series 5: Quantum & Information

Bayesian probability spaces, Shannon entropy, quantum logic lattices, and thermal density operators (ρ).
